citation: Pacalioga, J. O., Linaugo, J. D., Menes, C. C., Patiluna, M. L. E., Turbanos, F. M., & Bucol, A. A. (2010). Fishes and Macroinvertebrates of Bago River, Negros Occidental, Philippines. Silliman Journal, 51(1), January–June 2010.

accessReview.publisherRecord: Article record and a complete 25-page publisher-hosted issue PDF were reviewed. The article appears on printed pages 53–76 of Volume 51(1), January–June 2010. The article page download route currently returns 404; the alternate official journal host serves the PDF.
accessReview.fieldwork: Six months across wet season July–September 2009 and dry season February–April 2010.
accessReview.availableStructure: The article includes Table 1, a fish checklist with source ecological categories and presence marks for four study stations in both wet and dry seasons. Names and matrix cells have not been transcribed into repository data.
accessReview.reuse: The journal policy states that copyright is held by the journal and individual authors and specifies written permission for certain reproductions. No open license or permission to publish a structured derivative checklist was verified. Seek written guidance before extracting or distributing Table 1 data.

evidenceScope.waterbody: Bago River, Negros Occidental, Philippines; four selected stations along a headwater-to-mouth transect, not a complete inventory of every reach or tributary.
evidenceScope.collectionMethods: Article abstract describes cast nets, gillnets, hook-and-line, local gears called garab and taon, and hand picking for aquatic organisms.
evidenceScope.tableDesign: Fish records are organized by source-era ecological category and source-name label, with station-by-season marks. These marks represent the historical study table, not current occupancy.
evidenceScope.crossSourceRichness: The 2010 primary-paper abstract text says 55 fishes; a 2014 Bioflux paper independently cites Bago as 55 species in 33 families; the 2011 Señora River paper cites 56 species in 33 families. The 55 figure has independent corroboration, but the discrepancy remains unresolved and no value is used as a completion denominator.
evidenceScope.sourceEraClassification: The table separates primary freshwater, secondary freshwater, migratory and sporadic visitor groups. These historical classifications require current taxonomic/ecological review and should not be interpreted as present-day introduction status or habitat suitability.

decision.use: High-value historical primary source for Bago River station- and season-linked fish evidence, pending visual row verification, current taxonomy review and rights clarification.
decision.reason: The observed fish table is available but has not been visually transcribed; a 55-versus-56 source-level richness discrepancy remains; publication-platform and issue dates differ; and structured-data reuse terms are unresolved.

limitations: Evidence is from 2009–2010 and cannot establish present-day occupancy or current catchability.
Four purposively selected stations do not constitute a complete river, basin or regional species inventory.
The source includes fish categorized as freshwater, migratory or sporadic visitor taxa; freshwater catchment scope must remain explicit.
The article page displays a 2022 platform date while the issue PDF is dated 2010; use the issue date for the study.
No open license or structured data publication permission has been verified.
No species table rows, station geometries, current occurrences, safety or fishing-rule claims are created by this access review.
The 2014 Bugang paper repeats a Bago total of 55 species in 33 families, but the 2011 Señora paper cites 56; do not use a total until the primary table and citation are reconciled.
nextActions: Seek written guidance or permission from the journal and authors before extracting a structured Table 1 dataset.
If authorized, visually verify every species label and wet/dry station mark, then preserve source spellings separately from current accepted-name proposals.
Reconcile the primary-table total with both later citations (55 species in a 2014 paper versus 56 in the 2011 Señora paper), consulting original records if available.
Keep source-era ecological categories separate from present-day native, introduced, migratory, habitat, safety and legal status.
Continue other Negros and Siquijor river and lake source review without converting this site-level study into island-wide coverage.

references.supports: Official article record, authors, abstract and issue metadata.
Official full 25-page journal PDF, 2010 issue, field seasons, four study stations and fish table structure.
Journal copyright ownership and permission policy; no open structured-data license identified.
Later 2011 Señora River paper cites a Bago richness comparison of 56 species in 33 families.
Later Bugang River article independently cites Bago River as 55 species in 33 families and is already registered as bioflux-2014-bugang-river-fish-inventory.
